facts.claim: First detection of gravitational waves from a black hole merger (GW150914), confirming a binary black hole system.
Mass of the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way (Sagittarius A*) based on stellar orbits.
First direct image of a black hole shadow (M87*) captured by the Event Horizon Telescope.
Distance to the black hole M87* from Earth.
Radius of the event horizon (Schwarzschild radius) for a stellar-mass black hole of 10 solar masses.
Number of black hole mergers detected by LIGO/Virgo as of the third observing run (O3).
Year Stephen Hawking proposed that black holes emit radiation (Hawking radiation).
Predicted temperature of a solar-mass black hole due to Hawking radiation.
Number of black holes discovered in a study of gravitational wave data (catalog GWTC-3).
Speed of light limit for escape from a black hole's event horizon (escape velocity > c).
Year Karl Schwarzschild derived the first exact solution of Einstein's field equations describing a black hole.
Year the first stellar-mass black hole, Cygnus X-1, was confirmed (discovered 1964, confirmed via orbit).
Mass of Cygnus X-1's black hole (updated from parallax measurements).

hook_ideas: What if a black hole is a place where time becomes a direction, not a stream?
The first image of a black hole was a blurry orange ring – but it took 10,000 scientists and a telescope the size of Earth.
Your hair falls into a black hole and turns into a paradox – that's called the 'information paradox'.
The nearest known black hole is only about 1,500 light-years away – but it's invisible.
If you fell into a black hole, you'd be 'spaghettified' – but the universe might never see it happen due to time dilation.
misconceptions: Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners – they only pull things in within a certain radius; orbits at a distance are stable.
Not all black holes have an 'event horizon' that you can see – we only infer them from their effects on light and matter.
The 'nothing escapes' rule applies to the event horizon, but quantum effects (Hawking radiation) suggest black holes slowly lose mass.
Black holes do not 'suck' – they warp spacetime; matter falls in only if it has insufficient angular momentum to orbit.
The 'where space ends' framing is misleading – a black hole is a region of spacetime, not a boundary in space.
